blocks.text: To pass on to other points: in Isaiah and Jeremiah, יענה jaana is described as a bird that is Φιλέρημος [philerēmos], one that is accustomed to live in dry and waterless places. This plainly expresses the nature of the ostrich, which Theophrastus, in the place cited above, asserts ^{d)} is born chiefly ἐν τῇ μὴ ὑομένῃ τῆς Λιβύης [en tē mē hyomenē tēs Libyēs], in the waterless part of Libya: namely the one of which the Poet says,
On this side a region desert from thirst. —

On these words Servius comments: That is, uninhabitable. He means Xero-Libya, that is, the dry part of Africa that lies between Tripolis and Pentapolis. Quite correctly: for around these places were the Garamantes, who, Lucian says in the Dipsads, hunt [col. 227] wild asses, ostriches, apes, and elephants. Ταῦτα γὰρ μόνα, he says, διαρκεῖ πρὸς τὸ δίψος [tauta gar mona diarkei pros to dipsos]. For these animals alone endure thirst. This is true above all of the ostrich. For the Arabs, to whom this bird is very well known, deny that it ever drinks. Damir: قال ابن خالوية في كتاب ليس في الدنيا حيوان لا يسمع الا النعام ولا يشرب الما ابدا الا النعام والضب ايضا لا يشرب الما ولكنه يسمع [qāla Ibn Khālawayh fī kitāb Laysa fī al-dunyā ḥayawān lā yasmaʿ illā al-naʿām wa-lā yashrab al-mā abadan illā al-naʿām wa-al-ḍabb ayḍan lā yashrab al-mā wa-lākinnahu yasmaʿ] Ibno Chaluia said in the book Laisa (as if to say, in the book THERE IS NOT, for that book treats of things that do not exist in some thing or some place): There is no (perfect) animal that does not hear and that never drinks water, except the ostrich alone: for though the land crocodile also abstains from drinking, it nevertheless hears. Since, therefore, the ostrich needs no drink and devours anything whatever, it easily lives in waterless and barren places. Not without reason does Jerome, on Isaiah, say that it is an animal always seeking solitude and at home in the desert. And Basil: Φιλέρημον δὲ τὸ ζῶον, καὶ ταῖς ἀγονοτάταις ψάμμοις ὡς τὰ πολλὰ ἐμφωλεύων· τὴν οὖν ὑπερβολὴν τῆς ἐρημίας ὁ λόγος διὰ τῆς τῶν στρουθοκαμήλων σκηνώσεως παραδίδωσι· [philerēmon de to zōon, kai tais agonotatais psammois hōs ta polla emphōleuōn; tēn oun hyperbolēn tēs erēmias ho logos dia tēs tōn strouthokamēlōn skēnōseōs paradidōsi] It is a solitary animal, and mostly lurks in the most barren sands: hence Scripture signifies the desolation of the desert by the dwelling of ostriches. [II, 824] To the habits of ostriches also belong these words of Jeremiah, Thren. IV, 3: The sea monsters draw out the breast to suckle their young: but the daughter of my people is cruel, כיענים במדבר, like ostriches in the desert. The subject is the Israelites, whom the Babylonian captivity had reduced to such want that they could in no way provide for their children. Accordingly he adds in the next verse: The tongue of the suckling cleaves to his palate for thirst: and for the little ones asking for bread there is no one to distribute it. So too he had said in chapter 2, verse 9: that children perish of hunger at every street corner. That is, as R. Selomo rightly has it here, חייהם קודמים להם לחיי בניהם מחמת הרעב, In extreme hunger they preferred their own life to the life of their children. To heighten this hardness of the parents, the prophet uses a double comparison: one drawn from the sea monsters, which, monstrous as they are, still suckle their young; the other from the ostrich, which has so bad a name precisely because it neglects its offspring, as is said in Iob. XXXIX, 17. She shows herself hard toward her young, as if they were not hers ^{(3)}. We shall discuss this more fully in the explanation of that passage. So far, then, everything fits. And whatever the prophets write about the daughters of יענה jaana suits ostriches exactly.
